task: Write a cold email to a local coffee shop owner offering a tool that drafts replies to their customer emails.
rewrite:
ambition: A top cold emailer wouldn't send a generic pitch. They'd open with one specific, true detail about this shop. Then they'd show the tool's work by including a sample reply to a realistic customer email, such as a catering inquiry or a lost-item question. The email stays under about 100 words and ends with one low-effort ask.

agency: The rawest material is the shop's own public footprint. That means its website and contact page, its Google and Yelp reviews (especially ones the owner replied to, or didn't), its Instagram bio, and any "email us for catering or events" line. I'd read these directly and not work from a template or a list-vendor summary. The owner's name and the kind of email customers send come from there.

acceleration: Use a proven cold-email structure: a subject line under 6 words, a one-line personalized opener, a one-sentence problem, a one-sentence proof, and a single yes/no ask. Draft the sample reply with the tool itself, so the email is also a demo. Use a mail-merge or plain-text send, not a designed template, so it reads as one person writing to another.

accuracy: Nothing outside the model can confirm the email will work before it's sent. The closest proxies are:
- Every factual claim about the shop (name, menu item, review quote) checked against its public page.
- The sample reply read by one real small-business owner or barista, who says whether they'd send it.
- The email passing a CAN-SPAM check: real sender identity, physical address, and an opt-out line.
- After sending, reply rate on a small first batch is the real test.

**Subject:** Getting your evenings back from customer emails

Hi [Owner's name],

I'm [Your name], and I [live / work] near [neighborhood]. I'm a regular fan of [Coffee Shop], and the [specific drink or pastry] is the best in town.

Cafés like yours get a steady stream of emails: catering requests, questions about hours or oat milk, event bookings, and the occasional complaint. They usually get answered at 10pm after a long shift, or they don't get answered at all.

I built a small tool that drafts replies to those emails in your voice. It reads the message, pulls in your hours, menu, and policies, and writes a reply that's ready to go. You read it, tweak it if you want, and hit send. Nothing goes out without your approval.

Most owners I've talked to spend 3-5 hours a week on email. This should cut that to a fraction.

I'd like you to try it free for two weeks, and I'll set it up myself so you don't have to. If it doesn't save you time, you've lost nothing.

Would a 15-minute chat next week work, or could I stop by the shop at a quiet time? I'll bring my own coffee order, though I'd rather buy yours.

Thanks,
[Your name]
[Phone] | [Website or email]

---

**Notes:**
- Fill in the bracketed spots. The specific compliment in the first line matters most for getting a reply.
- If you have a real example, such as a reply the tool drafted for a catering inquiry, add it as a two-line sample.
- Don't claim the "3-5 hours" figure unless you can back it up. Swap in your own number or drop the sentence.

I also noticed the Google Drive connector needs authorization through your claude.ai connector settings before I can use it. I didn't need it for this email.
answers.nudge:
# Cold email: reply-drafting tool for a coffee shop owner

## Subject line options
1. Your catering inquiries at [Shop Name]
2. Quick question about your inbox, [First Name]
3. Replies to customer emails in 30 seconds

Option 1 is the strongest if you can check that they take catering or event inquiries. Otherwise use option 2.

## Main email (about 120 words)

**Subject:** Your catering inquiries at [Shop Name]

Hi [First Name],

I'm a regular at [Shop Name]. [One specific detail, e.g. "The cardamom latte is the reason I walk the long way to work."]

I noticed you list [email address] for [catering / custom orders / wholesale / events]. Running a shop, those emails probably get answered at 10pm or not at all.

I built a small tool that reads each customer email and drafts a reply in your voice. It uses your hours, menu, prices, and policies. You read the draft, tweak it if you want, and hit send. Nothing goes out without your approval.

Would you be open to me setting it up with your last 10 emails so you can judge the drafts yourself? It's free, takes about 15 minutes, and you owe me nothing after.

Either way, thanks for the great coffee.

[Your name]
[Phone] · [Neighborhood / "a few blocks from you"]

## Why it's written this way
- **Opens as a customer, not a vendor.** Owners ignore pitches but read notes from regulars.
- **Names a specific pain.** Late-night replies and missed inquiries are real for owners. "Save time with AI" is not.
- **Addresses the fear up front.** The line "nothing goes out without your approval" answers the worry that it will say something wrong to a customer.
- **Asks for a small trial, not a sale.** Running their own past emails through it lets them see the value without a demo or a call.
- **Ends with gratitude.** It gives them an easy, friendly way to say no.

## Follow-ups
**Day 4 (2–3 lines):**
> Hi [First Name], bumping this in case it got buried. Here's an example of what a draft looks like for a catering question: [paste a short before/after]. Happy to run yours if you'd like.

For the example, use a made-up customer email and a draft that sounds like a warm, brief human. Don't use a real customer's message.

**Day 10 (breakup):**
> Hi [First Name], I'll stop cluttering your inbox. If answering emails ever becomes a bottleneck, my offer stands. Thanks again for the coffee.

## Before you send
1. **Personalize the first line for real.** Visit, buy something, and note one true detail. Without that, the email reads as a template.
2. **Send to the owner's direct address**, not info@, if you can find it. The shop's Instagram bio or Google listing often has it.
3. **Send Tuesday–Thursday, 1–3pm**, after the lunch rush and before closing.
4. **Prepare the demo first.** Write 3–4 realistic sample emails (catering quote, "are you open Sunday?", a complaint, a lost-item question) with good drafts. That lets you reply to a "yes" within minutes.
5. **Handle data honestly.** Before you touch real customer emails, tell them where the emails are processed and stored, and let them opt out. Local owners talk to each other, so one bad experience costs you the whole neighborhood.
6. **Cap it at about 20 shops per week**, each personally researched. That beats 200 blasts.
7. **Compliance:** Include your real name and contact details, as above. If you're in the US, CAN-SPAM requires a physical address and an opt-out for commercial email. A short line like "Not interested? Just reply 'no thanks' and I won't write again" covers the opt-out.

## If you want to charge later
Offer 30 days free after the trial, then a flat monthly price (for example $20–40) with no contract. Owners trust a flat price more than per-use pricing.

I can tailor this to a specific shop if you give me its name and what you know about it. I can also write a version for text or Instagram DMs, or a one-page handout to leave at the counter.

Separately, the Google Drive connector in this session needs authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings. I didn't need it for this task, but it's unavailable until you do.
